newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Lebed to visit Brussels heart of old enemy NATO.
newsitem.headline: Lebed to visit Brussels heart of old enemy NATO.

text.p: Russia's controversial security chief Alexander Lebed arrives in Belgium on Sunday for a visit that will bring him face-to-face with his former Cold War foes at NATO's headquarters.

Lebed, a harsh critic of NATO's expansion plans, will hold two days of intensive -- and potentially explosive -- meetings at the political and military heart of the organisation created to defeat the former Soviet Union in a war that never happened.

NATO diplomats have been busily preparing the ground for the Lebed's first trip to Western Europe, but -- perhaps steeling themselves for a spectacular misfire -- are stressing the informal, almost fact-finding nature, of his mission.

"This is not a negotiating session, it is a contact-making, open discussion... NATO is an open institution and he will have the freedom of the house. He will be able to go anywhere he wants," one NATO official said.

He emphasised that the meeting was following on the heels of recent sessions with Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and Defence Minister Igor Rodionov and fell within the broader aim of building a new NATO-Russia relationship.

Lebed, who is President Boris Yeltsin's national security adviser, will hold six hours of talks on Monday at NATO's sprawling Brussels headquarters, meeting Secretary-General Javier Solana and the ambassadors of NATO's 16 members.

On Tuesday, he will visit its military headquarters at Mons in southern Belgium, where he will meet the alliance top brass including the Supreme Allied Commander in Europe (SACEUR) four-star U.S. General George Joulwan.
NATO officials and diplomats are looking forward to a constructive exchange of views.
Lebed seems all but certain to repeat his view, shared by Russia's entire political elite, that NATO's plans to take in new members from former communist eastern and central Europe are unacceptable.

But it is the force with which he says it, that will be most eagerly watched and disected by the alliance's Russian experts, who are waiting for signals that their bait of a new deal with Russia to run in parallel with expansion has gained some favour.

Last week Lebed, a 46-year-old former paratroop general who says he was not allowed out of the Soviet Union except to visit Afghanistan because he knew too many secrets, showed no sign of lessening his opposition to enlargement.
"NATO's expansion will take us back to hostility and to the spirit of confrontation," he told reporters, adding: "We have missiles, which are rusty but still effective, as a deterrent argument."
Solana said last week he was not expecting to change Lebed's mind in 24 hours, but hoped the talks would help convince the Russians that the alliance and expansion represented no threat to Moscow.
"I will try and put the emphasis on what we are doing together," Solana told reporters after addressing the European Parliament in Brussels last Wednesday.
Solana said he would raise Russia's continued participation in the NATO-led peace mission in Bosnia, likely to be extended for another year when its mandate expires next December.
Russia has a liasion officer at Mons to help coordinate its participation in the implementation force (IFOR) in Bosnia.
Lebed will visit him and the operation room for the mission in Bosnia, the same one which NATO's planners used to plot the destruction of the Soviet Union.
He will also meet the president of the upper and lower house of Belgium's parliament and the country defence minister Jean-Pol Poncelet.
